content.text: Hot reload swaps new code into the running app and rebuilds the widget tree, but everything already in memory stays:
objects, global and static variables, the screen you navigated to.

and initializers that already ran don't run again. A screen that works after a hot reload is new code running on old state; only a hot restart or a fresh launch shows how it behaves from a cold start.
A developer adds infinite scroll to the feed: one
, save, scroll down. Nothing loads. Hot reload "ignored"
, so they move the line into

, save again, and it works. Two weeks later, the backend team asks why every scroll near the bottom of the feed fires the same page request several times. The code was tested, just not the way it would run on a user's phone.
The belief: hot reload re-runs the app with the new code, only faster. So if the screen works after a hot reload, it will work when someone opens the app from scratch.
It's easy to believe because, for most UI work, that's exactly how it feels. You change a color or a padding in
, save, and the screen updates in about a second without losing your place. The console reports something like
, which sounds like a complete reload. And on the web, "reload" has always meant a fresh start. The catch is in the part that isn't visible: what hot reload deliberately leaves alone.
Hot reload patches code, then rebuilds

recompiles the libraries you changed, plus the main library and the libraries that lead to them, into kernel files and sends them to the Dart VM running your app. The VM loads the new code, and at that point no code has been re-executed yet. Then the framework rebuilds, re-lays out and repaints every existing widget and render object. Only code involved in rebuilding the widget tree runs again. It works only in debug mode.
Everything the app built up before the reload survives it. Put together with the docs' special cases, your code falls into four groups:

items.text: method and whatever it calls. Changed function bodies take effect the next time they're called, and changes to
objects and their fields, the navigation stack, and global variables and static fields, which the docs say are treated as state and not reinitialized.

: native Kotlin, Java, Swift or Objective-C code, which needs a full restart, plus a few type-level changes such as turning an enum into a class or changing a generic type's parameters.

content.text: The docs also warn that when code changes affect your app's state, the data it works with after a reload might not match what it would have if it had run from scratch. You logged in an hour ago, opened three screens and filled a cache. Your new code now runs against all of that. A bug that only appears on a clean launch, with no user, an empty cache or a different first screen, stays hidden.

blocks.title: Debug mode is not the app your users run

content.text: Hot reload exists only in debug mode, where assertions are enabled and compilation is optimized for fast development cycles, not execution speed. Release builds disable assertions and are compiled for fast startup and execution. A smooth session full of hot reloads tells you nothing about startup time, performance or a cold launch. Check those in profile or release mode on a real device.
